lesson.title: Remembering to Remember: Prospective Memory
lesson.summary: Prospective memory is the explicit ability to remember to carry out an intended action at some point in the future, whether triggered by a specific time or by an environmental cue.
lesson.body:
Prospective memory is the explicit memory system responsible for remembering to carry out an intended action at some point in the future, rather than remembering something that already happened. Deciding to call a friend back later, take medication at a scheduled time, or drop off a package on the way to work all depend on prospective memory. Because forming that intention and later recognizing the right moment to act on it both require conscious, deliberate awareness, prospective memory belongs to the explicit memory system rather than the implicit one, even though its content, a plan for the future, is quite different from the facts and past events typically associated with explicit memory.

Psychologists usually distinguish two types of prospective memory based on what triggers retrieval. Event-based prospective memory is triggered by an external cue in the environment, such as remembering to give a friend a message the next time you happen to see them, or remembering to mail a letter as soon as a mailbox comes into view. Time-based prospective memory, by contrast, is triggered by reaching a particular point in time, such as remembering to call someone at three o'clock, with no environmental cue to prompt the memory. Time-based tasks tend to be more difficult because they require a person to self-generate the reminder by periodically checking the time, rather than relying on the world to hand them a cue.

Prospective memory involves two distinct phases that make it different from ordinary explicit recall. First, a person has to form and encode the intention itself, deciding what needs to be done and, ideally, when or where it should happen. Second, and often the harder part, the person must later notice the appropriate moment and retrieve that intention while they are busy doing something else entirely. Unlike a typical explicit memory test, where someone directly asks a person to recall information, prospective memory has no one to prompt the retrieval. The rememberer has to interrupt their own ongoing activity at exactly the right moment, entirely on their own.

Consider someone who decides over breakfast to buy milk on the way home from work. The intention itself is easy enough to form and takes only a moment. The much harder task comes hours later, while driving home and thinking about the day's events, when the person has to notice, unprompted, that this is the moment the earlier intention applies to. If they drive straight past the store without the intention ever resurfacing, prospective memory has failed, not because the original plan was forgotten in the sense of being erased, but because it was never retrieved at the moment it was needed.

Prospective memory failures are extremely common in daily life and tend to increase whenever attention is divided or cognitive demands are high, which is part of why missed medication doses, forgotten errands, and overlooked appointments happen so often even to people with generally reliable memories. Because time-based tasks are especially hard to self-monitor, people frequently convert them into easier event-based tasks by building an external cue into the environment, setting an alarm, placing an object by the front door, or leaving a sticky note where it will be seen at the right moment. These strategies work by offloading the burden of self-generated monitoring onto a reliable external trigger instead.
